claims.text: Arc-melted HfNbTiVAl10 exhibits a hierarchical heterostructure.
Minor VEC-guided compositional adjustments can tune the hierarchical heterostructural features of HfNbTiVAl10.
Tuning those features can enable models that predict Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture behavior more rapidly and accurately than established simulations.
Selective enrichment of Ta or V and depletion of other elements can modify the atomic environment controlling heterostructure formation.
Nanoscale and microscale interphase interfaces in the hierarchical heterostructure mediate load transfer.
Nanoscale and microscale interphase interfaces mediate crack propagation.
Minor compositional variations alter electron concentration.
Changes in electron concentration modify phase formation in the hierarchical structure.
Changes in electron concentration modify phase connectivity in the hierarchical structure.
Changes in phase formation and connectivity affect interphase strength.
Changes in phase formation and connectivity affect intrinsic deformation mechanisms.
Composition-adjusted microstructural features can be quantitatively related to macroscopic mechanical responses.
The proposed models will require roughly half the computational or simulation time of the baseline methods.
The proposed models will reduce prediction error by approximately 20% for Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture behavior.
The baseline established methods rely solely on microstructural image analysis and 3D phase-field models without detailed VEC-driven heterostructural modulation.
The approach may fail when processing variables or inherent defects dominate microstructural evolution.
The approach may fail if electron count does not reliably correlate with mechanical-property variations in HfNbTiVAl10.
Direct correlation data connecting VEC modifications to hierarchical-structure evolution in HfNbTiVAl10 are limited.
Modified and unmodified batches are to be tested under identical room-temperature tensile and fracture conditions.
Failure to achieve at least 50% faster prediction and at least 20% lower prediction error with statistical significance is declared falsifying.

contradictions.description: The initial alloy contains no Ta, so 'enriching' Ta would actually add a new component and create a different alloy system, whereas the experiment continues to describe the modified batches as HfNbTiVAl10.

The outcome uses 'roughly halved computational time,' while the falsification rule uses 'at least 50% faster.' These are not mathematically identical unless 'faster' is explicitly defined as percent time reduction.
